u00.l01.title: Tone changes the word
objectives: Pattern: the same letters with different tones are different words
Hear high and low tone on the same spelling
Tell àkwà, ákwà, àkwá and ákwá apart by ear

note.title: Tone changes the word
note.pattern: Two tones and a step down
note.body: Every Igbo syllable has a tone: high (á), low (à) or a downstepped high (ā), a high said a little lower than the high before it. Everyday writing leaves tones out, so you learn words by ear; the course shows the marks in a separate pronunciation layer.

u00.l02.title: Two words, one spelling
objectives: Pattern: high-high and high-low can be different words

note.title: Two words, one spelling
note.body: In these pairs the first syllable is the same and only the last one moves: up for one word, down for the other. Listen for where the voice ends.

u00.l03.title: Three tones, three words
objectives: Pattern: the downstep is a third tone shape
Hear the high, low and downstepped tones of igwe
Hear ísí (head), ísì (smell) and ìsì (blindness) apart

note.title: Three tones, three words
note.body: A downstepped high (marked with a macron, ā) comes after a high and sounds a step lower, but still high. It cannot start a word or follow a low.

u00.l04.title: Dots make different vowels
objectives: Pattern: ị ọ ụ are their own vowels, never i o u with a mistake
Read and hear four words with dotted vowels
Type ị, ọ, ụ with the key strip

note.title: Dots make different vowels
note.body: Igbo has eight vowels: a e i ị o ọ u ụ. The dot under ị, ọ and ụ makes a different vowel, said with the tongue root pulled back, and ṅ (with a dot above) is its own consonant, like the ng in 'sing'. Course text never drops a dot; when you type one without its dot the app only reminds you.

u00.l05.title: Light and heavy vowels
objectives: Notice which set a word's vowels come from

note.title: Light and heavy vowels
note.pattern: Vowel harmony: {a ị ọ ụ} and {e i o u}
note.body: Igbo vowels come in two sets. Most simple words use vowels from one set only, and small words that attach to a verb (pronouns, prefixes) change to match the verb's set. You will meet this rule again in every verb lesson.

u00.l06.title: Letters written with two
objectives: Pattern: nine consonants are written with two letters

note.title: Letters written with two
note.pattern: ch gb gh gw kp kw nw ny sh
note.body: Nine Igbo consonants are written with two letters but are one sound. kp and gb are made with the lips and the back of the tongue closing at the same time; practise them slowly.

u00.l07.title: m and n on their own
objectives: Pattern: m and n can be a syllable with a tone
Hear mmiri, nkịta and the two mma

note.title: m and n on their own
note.body: Before a consonant, m and n are a syllable of their own and carry a tone, so mmiri has three syllables. Hum the first sound on its own pitch before you open the vowel.

u00.l08.title: Four words called oke
objectives: Pattern: all four tone shapes on one spelling
Hear óké, òkè, ókè and òké apart

note.title: Four words called oke
note.body: Like akwa, the letters oke make four different words. Say each one slowly, then fast; the tone trainer mixes them with the other sets.

u00.l09.title: Review: sounds and letters
objectives: Hear and tell apart the tone sets
Read and type the dotted vowels

u01.l01.title: Hello, how are you?
objectives: Pattern: Kedụ ka i mere? and its answer
Ask how someone is, and answer

note.title: Hello, how are you?
note.body: In the question, the word for 'you' takes the vowel set of the verb after it, so it is the undotted i before mere. The usual answer says 'it is good'.
note.culture: Greet first, and greet older people before they greet you. A greeting is not small talk: skipping it can read as rude.

note.title: Thank you, welcome, goodbye
note.body: Greetings are learned whole: you do not need to take them apart to use them. Nnọọ is said to someone who arrives; Daalụ thanks.

u01.l03.title: Names and what they mean
objectives: Pattern: an Igbo name is a short sentence
Hear and say six common Igbo names

note.title: Names and what they mean
note.body: Most Igbo names are short sentences or phrases about God, family or the circumstances of a birth. Asking what a name means is a friendly question.

u01.l04.title: Morning and night
objectives: Pattern: greetings by the time of day
Name the morning and the night
Say good morning and good night

note.title: Morning and night
note.body: Morning and night greetings are fixed expressions. The good-morning word here is the dataset's; many speakers also greet with other forms, which you will hear in the regional recordings.

note.title: Please, sorry, yes and no
note.pattern: Ndo is sympathy, not only apology
note.body: Ndo is said whenever something bad happens to someone (a fall, a loss, a hard day), not only when it is your fault. Biko comes before or after a request.

u01.l06.title: Goodbye and respect
objectives: Address an older man with respect

note.title: Goodbye and respect
note.body: A younger person adds a word of respect when greeting an older one. The word here is for an older man; ask the people around you which forms they use for older women.
note.culture: Respect for age runs through Igbo greetings: the younger greets first, often with a title of respect.

u01.l07.title: Review: greetings
objectives: Answer yes, no, please and sorry

u01.placement.title: Listening check
objectives: Find out how much you already understand

u02.l01.title: The four market days
objectives: Pattern: the izu, a week of four market days
Name the four market days of the Igbo week in order
Hear how a market day can be said in another area

note.title: The four market days
note.body: The traditional Igbo week (izu) has four market days. Towns hold their markets on particular days, so the day names are part of everyday plans.
note.culture: Each market day was also linked to a deity in the traditional religion; Okwu teaches only the names of the days.

u02.l02.title: Around the village
objectives: Pattern: places are nouns you can point to
Name the places of the village
Say where the market, the farm and the stream are

note.title: Around the village
note.body: These nouns are the places of the Obodo you are restoring. They do not change for one or many.

u02.l03.title: What grows on the farm
objectives: Name four crops of the farm

note.title: What grows on the farm
note.body: Yam is the prestige crop, celebrated at the New Yam festival. Cocoyam, maize and pumpkin leaf are everyday crops.

u02.l05.title: Buying and selling
objectives: Say who sells and who bought

note.title: Buying and selling
note.body: The verb for selling appears with na- in front (someone is selling, sells). Bought is a past form: the verb takes an ending that copies its vowel. Unit 9 explains both; here, learn them as phrases.

u02.l06.title: Things at the market
objectives: Name pepper, salt, oil and fish

note.title: Things at the market
note.body: These are things you find at every market. Fish (ázụ̀) and back (àzụ́) share their letters: listen to the tones.

u02.l04.title: A story: Eke market day
objectives: Read and hear a short story about going to the market

comprehension.question: What does the speaker's mother do?

u02.l07.title: Review: market day
objectives: Name the market days, places and crops

u03.l01.title: My name is
objectives: Pattern: Aha m bụ … (my name is …)

note.title: My name is
note.pattern: aha m: the owner comes after
note.body: Igbo puts the owner after the thing: 'name my'. bụ links two things that are the same: my name is Nneka. To ask, put the question word first.

note.title: Who are you?
note.body: With 'I' as the subject, a prefix a- or e- (matching the verb's vowel set) joins the verb, and m comes after it: I am. Onye with a low first tone asks 'who?'; with a high first tone it means 'person'.

u03.l03.title: Where are you from?
objectives: Say what town or country you are from

note.title: Where are you from?
note.pattern: onye obodo m: 'a person of my town'
note.body: To say where someone is from, Igbo often says they are a person of that place. ebee asks 'where?'.

u03.l04.title: Names that praise God
objectives: Hear four names and what they mean

note.title: Names that praise God
note.body: Many names begin with Chi or Chukwu (God) and say something about God: God has done much, God gave. The meaning is part of the name's beauty.

u03.l05.title: Born on a market day
objectives: Pattern: Oke- and Mgb- + market day
Hear names given for the day of birth

note.title: Born on a market day
note.body: A boy born on a market day may be named Oke- plus the day, a girl Mgb- plus the day: Okeeke, Mgbeeke. The girls' forms are now rare (the dataset calls them archaic).
note.culture: Market-day names keep the four-day week alive in families.

u03.l06.title: Meeting someone new
objectives: Greet, ask a name and answer in a short dialogue

note.title: Meeting someone new
note.pattern: Adị m mma: I am well
note.body: dị describes a state; with 'I' it takes the a- prefix and m: I am (well). Compare bụ, which says what someone is.

u03.l07.title: Review: names and me
objectives: Say who you are and where you are from

u04.l01.title: Mother and father
objectives: Talk about what your mother is doing

note.title: Mother and father
note.body: 'My mother' is mother + m. The same small word m means 'me' after a verb.

note.title: Brothers and sisters
note.body: Igbo has one word for brother or sister; add the word for man or woman after it to be specific.

u04.l03.title: My, your, his, our
objectives: Pattern: possessive words after the noun
Say your mother, his father, our house

note.title: My, your, his, our
note.pattern: m, gị, ya, anyị, unu, ha
note.body: The possessive comes after the noun: my (m), your (gị), his or her (ya), our (anyị), your all (unu), their (ha). They are written as separate words.

note.title: Husband and wife
note.body: Where English uses an adjective (pretty, kind), Igbo often uses a verb or a verb phrase. Learn the whole phrase.

note.title: Grandparents and in-laws
note.body: The grandparent words are built from father and mother plus 'big'. In many places other forms are used too: listen to the regional recordings.
note.culture: Family reaches far beyond the household: in-laws, the father's kindred and the mother's people all have their place and their respect.

u04.l06.title: A story: my family
objectives: Read and hear a short story about a family

comprehension.question: How many children did the mother have?
What is the mother doing now?

u04.l07.title: Review: family
objectives: Use my, your, his and our

note.title: One to four
note.body: Count out loud first; in a phrase the number comes after the thing counted.

note.title: Five to eight
note.body: Notice the long vowels in six and seven: each vowel is a syllable with its own tone.

note.title: Nine, ten and how many?
note.body: The number follows the noun: three houses is 'house three'. ole (how many?) goes in the same place.

note.title: Hundreds and thousands
note.body: Hundreds and thousands work like other numbers. Tens are built from ten: ten two (twenty) and so on.

note.title: How old are you?
note.body: Age uses dị (a state): my child is six years, 'child my is year six'. The question puts ole in the number's place.

note.title: How much is it?
note.body: To ask a price, ask how much money: the question word ole again.

u05.l07.title: Counting in twenties
objectives: Hear the traditional count in twenties
Tell three words spelled ọgụ apart

note.title: Counting in twenties
note.body: The traditional count groups by twenty (ọgụ): forty is two twenties. Many elders still use it for ages and yams. Listen also for the tones: ọgụ is also a hoe and a fight.
note.culture: Counting in twenties belonged to markets and farms; heritage learners may hear it from grandparents.

u06.l01.title: Food
objectives: Name food, soup, rice and cassava

note.title: Food
note.body: A meal is often a soup (ofe) eaten with a swallow made from cassava or yam. Rice is everyday food too.

u06.l02.title: In the kitchen
objectives: Pattern: na- + verb, someone is cooking
Name a pot, a plate and two soup leaves

note.title: In the kitchen
note.body: Many soups are named after their leaf: bitter leaf soup, utazi soup. The leaf name comes after the word for soup.

note.title: Eat and drink
note.body: Igbo usually names what is eaten: 'eat food'. A command uses the verb alone with a vowel ending: drink!

note.title: Meals of the day
note.body: Breakfast, lunch and dinner are food + morning, afternoon or night.

note.title: Welcome a guest
note.body: A host welcomes, offers a seat and then something to eat or drink, often kola first.
note.culture: A visitor is welcomed before anything else is discussed; refusing all hospitality can give offence.

note.title: Kola and palm wine
note.body: Kola is presented to guests with prayers and blessings, by custom by a man and in the language of the place. The saying here is from the dataset; its meaning and use are for the cultural advisor to confirm.
note.culture: Kola (ọjị) is a symbol of welcome and goodwill. Who breaks it and how follows local custom; Okwu teaches it as culture, never as a game object.

u06.l07.title: A story: the visitors
objectives: Read and hear a story about receiving visitors

u07.l01.title: Today, tomorrow, yesterday
objectives: Pattern: time words at the end

note.title: Today, tomorrow, yesterday
note.body: Time words usually come at the end of the sentence: they will come tomorrow.

u07.l02.title: Parts of the day
objectives: Say in the morning, afternoon, evening and at night

note.title: Parts of the day
note.body: 'In' or 'at' is na, written n' before a vowel: in the morning, at night. Before a consonant it stays na.

note.title: What time is it?
note.body: Clock time borrows elekere (clock) and a number: elekere isii, six o'clock.

note.title: Days, months and years
note.body: 'Every month' can be said with kwa before the noun or ọbụla after it.

u07.l05.title: The Igbo week
objectives: Know how izu and the seven-day week fit

note.title: The Igbo week
note.body: A market day used as a date is 'day' + the market day. Seven market weeks make a traditional month.
note.culture: The izu of four days (Eke, Orie, Afọ, Nkwọ) still sets market days and some ceremonies, next to the seven-day week used for school, work and church.

u07.l06.title: Now and always
objectives: Pattern: ugbu a, oge niile, kwa ụbọchị
Say now, every day and all the time

note.title: Now and always
note.body: Now (ugbu a) and all the time (oge niile) go at the end, like other time words.

u07.l07.title: A story: one day
objectives: Read and hear a day from morning to night

comprehension.question: When did the speaker come back?
What do they do at night?

u07.l08.title: Review: time and days
objectives: Use the market days as dates

note.title: Where is it?
note.pattern: Ebee ka ọ dị? 'where is it?'
note.body: ebee asks 'where'; ka links it to the rest. For things, use dị (is located); for people and animals, use nọ.

u08.l02.title: Places in town
objectives: Name the school, the hospital and the river

note.title: Places in town
note.body: Many buildings are named 'house of' + what happens there: the house of medicine is the hospital.

note.title: Left, right, front and back
note.body: Right and left are 'right hand' and 'left hand'. Back (àzụ́) and fish (ázụ̀) share their letters: listen for the tones.

note.title: In, on, under
note.body: na (in, at) becomes n' before a vowel: n'ime (inside), n'elu (on top), n'okpuru (under). It is written joined with an apostrophe.

u08.l05.title: Come and go
objectives: Pattern: commands with bịa and ga

note.title: Come and go
note.body: These motion verbs are the commonest commands: come here, go. lọta means to come back home.

note.title: Near and far
note.body: 'It is far' uses a verb phrase (tere aka); 'near' is dị nso. The answer to 'where are you going?' uses na- (I am going).

u08.l07.title: A story: to the river
objectives: Read and hear a story about a trip to the river

comprehension.question: What did they do at the river?

u09.l01.title: Doing it now: na-
objectives: Say what someone is doing now

note.title: Doing it now: na-
note.body: na- with a hyphen before the verb means the action is going on now or happens habitually. The verb starts with a vowel (a- or e-) that matches its vowel set: na-aga, na-eri. With 'I', say Ana m … (I am …).

note.title: Will do: ga-
note.body: ga- with a hyphen before the verb makes the future. With 'I', the prefix joins the auxiliary: Aga m … (I will …).

note.title: Did it: -rV
note.body: For action verbs, adding r plus a copy of the verb's vowel makes the past: ga → gara (went), ri → riri (ate), bịa → bịara (came). For state verbs the same ending means the present.

note.title: Has done: -la
note.body: The perfect (has done) adds -la (or -le, matching the verb) after the verb, and the subject's vowel prefix. Spelling of this suffix is under review (STYLE_GUIDE D1).

note.title: Do it!
note.body: A command uses the verb with a vowel ending that copies or matches its vowel: gaa (go), rie (eat), nye (give). Add biko to be polite.

u09.l06.title: Not: -ghị
objectives: Say what someone does not do or want

note.title: Not: -ghị
note.body: The negative adds a vowel prefix (a- or e-, matching the verb) and -ghị after the verb: Achọghị m (I don't want). 'Does not' in the present uses anaghị before the verb. Spelling: STYLE_GUIDE D1.

u09.l07.title: Don't!
objectives: Tell someone not to do something

note.title: Don't!
note.body: 'Don't …!' is a vowel prefix (a- or e-) + the verb + -la: Abịala (don't come). It looks like the perfect, but the context and the tones tell them apart.

note.title: God
note.body: Chukwu (the great God) and Chineke (God the creator) are names of God; chi is also a person's own guardian spirit, which is why it appears in so many names.
note.culture: chi is a personal guardian spirit in Igbo thought, and also a word for God in Christian usage. Teach it with respect for both.

note.title: At church
note.body: Going to church is 'going to ụka'. The priest or pastor is ụkọchukwu, 'servant of God'.

note.title: Blessings
note.pattern: Ka Chineke gọzie …: may God bless …
note.body: A blessing starts with ka (let, may) and the verb in its command form.

note.title: Christmas and festivals
note.body: You 'do' or 'celebrate' a festival with the verbs gba and eme.
note.culture: December is homecoming: families travel back to their towns for Christmas, weddings and meetings.

u10.l05.title: Custom and the masquerade
objectives: Name custom, culture and the masquerade respectfully

note.title: Custom and the masquerade
note.body: omenaala is custom, 'what is done in the land'. The masquerade (mmọnwụ) belongs to community festivals and has its own rules of respect.
note.culture: Masquerades are sacred in many communities: who may approach or speak about them follows local rules. Okwu presents them only as respected culture, never as avatars or rewards.

u10.l06.title: A story: Sunday
objectives: Read and hear a story about a church service

comprehension.question: What does the priest ask them to do?

note.title: Ears, nose and teeth
note.pattern: A tone pair in the body
note.body: Teeth and king share their letters: high-high for teeth, high-low for king.

u11.l02.title: The body
objectives: Name body, leg, belly and heart

note.title: The body
note.body: ahụ is the body, and many feeling phrases are built on it. Belly (áfọ́), year (áfọ̀) and the market day Àfọ̀ are a three-way tone set.

note.title: I'm not well
note.body: 'I have a headache' uses nwe (have) with the e- prefix and m. Being sick uses na- + rịa ọrịa (suffer an illness).

note.title: Happy and sad
note.body: Happiness and unhappiness are often said about the heart (obi): my heart is not good = I am not happy.

u11.l05.title: Angry, afraid, tired
objectives: Pattern: the feeling does it to you

note.title: Angry, afraid, tired
note.pattern: Iwe na-ewe m: 'anger is taking me'
note.body: Many feelings are the subject: anger takes you, fear frightens you, tiredness finishes you. The person comes after the verb.

u11.l06.title: A story: a sick day
objectives: Read and hear a story about someone who is ill

comprehension.question: Why didn't the friend see Ada?
What is better than treating an illness?

u12.l01.title: A wedding
objectives: Pattern: ịgba nkwụ, the traditional wedding
Talk about going to a wedding

note.title: A wedding
note.body: Many couples have a traditional wedding (ịgba nkwụ, 'carrying palm wine') and a church wedding (agbamakwụkwọ). The verb lụ (marry) takes di (a husband) or nwunye (a wife).
note.culture: At the traditional wedding the bride finds her groom in the crowd and offers him palm wine; details vary by town.

u12.l02.title: Music and celebration
objectives: Talk about music, dancing and a ceremony

note.title: Music and celebration
note.body: egwu is music or song; to dance is to 'play' (gba) egwu.

note.title: A new baby
note.body: A child's name is announced at a naming ceremony, often with the meaning explained. Aha nwa m … bụ … says what a child is called.
note.culture: Naming ceremonies differ by town and family; grandmothers often name children too, and a mother's care after birth (ọmụgwọ) is a cherished custom.

note.title: Condolences
note.body: Ndo (unit 1) is what you say to the bereaved, often repeated. Keep it short and stay close.
note.culture: Funerals are large community events, sometimes held long after a death. Visit, say ndo, and follow the family's lead.

note.title: Titles and honour
note.body: A titled man has 'taken' (chi) a title such as ọzọ. Respect (ùgwù) and mountain (úgwú) are spelled alike: listen for the tones.
note.culture: Titles are earned honours with duties; never use them as game rewards.

u12.l06.title: A story: the wedding
objectives: Read and hear a story about a wedding

comprehension.question: On which market day is the wedding?
What did they eat at the wedding?

u12.l07.title: Review: life events
objectives: Talk about weddings, births and titles

u13.l01.title: One word, many towns
objectives: Hear four words in several regional forms

note.title: One word, many towns
note.body: Every word card can show how it is said elsewhere. None is more correct: the standard form is the one shared in writing, and your family's form is yours.

u13.l02.title: r and l
objectives: Pattern: r in the standard, l in some areas

note.title: r and l
note.body: In Ọnịcha and much of Anambra, many words with r are said with l. Listen to the regional recordings of these words and of food and water from earlier units.

u13.l03.title: s and sh
objectives: Pattern: s in the standard, sh in some areas

note.title: s and sh
note.body: In Owere and some other areas, s in many words is said as sh. The tree word shows it clearly.

u13.l04.title: h, f and v
objectives: Pattern: h in the standard, f or v in some areas

note.title: h, f and v
note.body: Where the standard has h, some areas say f, v or another sound: market, thing and cow show it.

u13.l05.title: One and nine
objectives: Hear one and nine in regional forms

note.title: One and nine
note.body: One (otu) is ofu in some areas; nine has several forms (STYLE_GUIDE D6). Count the way your family does; the course keeps the standard for exercises.

objectives: Recognise regional forms of common words

akuko.ahia-eke.title: Eke market day
akuko.ahia-eke.summary: It is Eke market day. The speaker's mother is a trader and sends the speaker to buy two yams at the market, which is far; the speaker goes.

questions.question: What does the speaker's mother do?

akuko.ahu-adighi.title: A sick day
akuko.ahu-adighi.summary: Ada does not come out; her friend guesses she is unwell. She is sick, takes headache medicine, is told to take her medicine first, someone wants to heal her, her friend stays by her bed, and the story ends with a lesson about prevention.

narrative.text: Ada's friend notices that Ada is missing.
At Ada's house: Ada is ill and is taking medicine for her headache.
Her mother is firm: medicine first.
A nurse comes who wants to heal her.
Her friend stays at her bedside, which is a kindness.
Ada's grandmother has the last word.

questions.question: Why didn't the friend see Ada?
What is better than treating an illness?

akuko.ezinulo.title: My family
akuko.ezinulo.summary: The speaker describes the family: a palm-wine-tapper father, a teacher mother with five children, a brother who trades, a married sister, siblings at work and a mother cooking.

questions.question: How many children did the mother have?
What is the mother doing now?

akuko.igba-nkwu.title: The wedding
akuko.igba-nkwu.summary: Emeka is to marry Ada. The wedding is set for an Orie day and everyone wants it lively; the speaker travels to Enugu for the traditional wedding, where the husband's friends sing, people dance well and eat ngwọngwọ.

questions.question: On which market day is the wedding?
What did they eat at the wedding?

akuko.obia.title: The visitors
akuko.obia.summary: Visitors arrive unexpectedly. They are welcomed in and offered a seat while the host brings kola; the kola has four lobes. The mother entertains the guest, and the palm wine is sweet.

akuko.otu-ubochi.title: One day
akuko.otu-ubochi.summary: A day from morning to night: breakfast and a chat in the morning, play in the afternoon, coming home in the evening, soup and sleep at night.

questions.question: When did the speaker come back?
What do they do at night?

akuko.ubochi-uka.title: Sunday
akuko.ubochi-uka.summary: A Sunday service: the family goes to church, the service begins, everyone falls quiet as the priest comes in, Adanna sings hymns, the priest speaks and leads a prayer, and God answers prayer.

questions.question: What does the priest ask them to do?

akuko.uzo-osimiri.title: To the river
akuko.uzo-osimiri.summary: Chike and his friends spend a day at the river: the way there, fishing, fetching water, a lost ring and the walk home at night.

narrative.text: His friend gives directions for the path.
At the river the boys fish while a girl fetches water with a calabash.
The place for fetching water is close by.
Then someone's ring slips into the water.
They search, and only come home after dark.

questions.question: What did they do at the river?
